title: Clean Shutdown Flow
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Robotics and Computational Thinking
description: An interactive flowchart and robot scene that traces a MicroPython main loop through try, except KeyboardInterrupt, and finally when the user presses Ctrl+C or a sensor error occurs, showing that only the finally block reliably stops the motors.

educational.topic: Exception handling and clean shutdown with try, except, and finally
learningObjectives: Trace the path a MicroPython program takes through try, except KeyboardInterrupt, and finally when the user presses Ctrl+C.
Trace the path the program takes when an error that is not a KeyboardInterrupt occurs inside the try block.
Explain why motor shutdown code belongs in the finally block instead of the except block.
prerequisites: Writing a while True main loop
Reading indented code blocks and if/elif/else logic
Running and stopping a program in Thonny
standards: CSTA 2-AP-17: Systematically test and refine programs using a range of test cases

pedagogical.interactionPattern: Students trigger Ctrl+C or a sensor error; the highlight walks the flowchart one node at a time while the console and robot scene update.
keyQuestions: Which blocks run when you press Ctrl+C?
Which blocks run when a ValueError happens inside the try block?
Why does 'Motors off. Goodbye!' print before the error message?
What happens to the motors when there is no finally block?
commonMisconceptions: An except block catches every kind of error, not just the one it names.
When a program stops, the motors stop automatically.
The finally block only runs when there was no error.
Motor stop code in the except block is just as safe as motor stop code in finally.
assessmentOpportunities: Predict which blocks run before triggering each event, then compare with the highlighted path.
Challenge: with the finally block removed, cause a sensor error and describe what the robot does.
Exit ticket: identify which event still leaves the motors running if the stop code moves into except.
